A_target.statement:
Let $f$ be a [[Definition:Real Function|real function]] which is [[Definition:Continuous on Closed Interval|continuous]] on $\closedint a b$ and [[Definition:Differentiable on Interval|differentiable]] on $\openint a b$, with $\map f a = \map f b$.
Then:
:$\exists \xi \in \openint a b: \map {f'} \xi = 0$

B_source.statement:
Let $f$ be [[Definition:Continuous Real Function|continuous]] on $\closedint a b$.
Then $f$ attains a [[Definition:Maximum Value of Real Function|maximum]] and a [[Definition:Minimum Value of Real Function|minimum]] on $\closedint a b$.

substitutions.the attained extremes: candidates for an interior critical point

object_map.reformulation: Turn the search for a zero of the derivative into the search for an interior extremum of f.

validity_conditions: f must be continuous on the closed interval so that the extremes are attained.
Equal endpoint values are needed to force an extremum into the open interval.
Differentiability on the open interval is needed to apply Fermat's criterion at that extremum.
proof_plan: By the [[Extreme Value Theorem]], $f$ attains a maximum $M$ at some $x_1$ and a minimum $m$ at some $x_2$ in $\closedint a b$.
If $M = m$, then $f$ is [[Definition:Constant Mapping|constant]] on $\closedint a b$, so $\map {f'} \xi = 0$ for every $\xi \in \openint a b$.

Otherwise $M > m$.
As $\map f a = \map f b$, the values $M$ and $m$ cannot both be attained only at the endpoints, so one of $x_1, x_2$ lies in $\openint a b$; call it $\xi$.
